name: Linear Algebra True/False: Concepts
description: Conceptual true/false questions covering all exam topics: systems, subspaces, transformations, rank/nullity, eigenvalues, orthogonality, and more

questions.question: If the equation Ax=b has a unique solution for some vector b, then it has a unique solution for every b in R^n.
options: True, because if Ax=b has a unique solution for any b, then Ax=0 has only the trivial solution, meaning A is invertible and Ax=b has a unique solution for all b
True, because uniqueness for one specific b implies the columns of A are proportional, guaranteeing uniqueness for all other vectors as well
False, because uniqueness for one b depends on that particular b, and other vectors may lead to inconsistent or underdetermined systems
False, because Ax=b can only have a unique solution for all b when A is a symmetric matrix
questions.explanation: True. If Ax=b has a unique solution for some b, then the homogeneous system Ax=0 has only the trivial solution (no free variables). This means A has full rank and is invertible, so Ax=b has a unique solution for every b in R^n.

questions.question: If A is a 3x5 matrix and the system Ax=b is consistent, then the solution set must contain infinitely many solutions.
options: True, because all rectangular matrices produce infinitely many solutions regardless of consistency
True, because a 3x5 matrix has at most 3 pivots and at least 2 free variables, so any consistent system has a free variable and therefore infinitely many solutions
False, because even a 3x5 matrix can yield a unique solution if b is chosen to match a specific column
False, because the number of solutions depends only on the specific values in A, not its dimensions
questions.explanation: True. A 3x5 matrix has 5 columns but at most 3 pivot columns, so there are at least 2 free variables. Whenever the system is consistent, the free variables generate infinitely many solutions.

questions.question: The columns of every 5x3 matrix are linearly dependent.
options: True, because a matrix with more rows than columns always has linearly dependent columns due to dimensional excess
True, because columns of any non-square matrix cannot be independent since they live in a larger space than there are columns
False, because columns are dependent only when the matrix has more columns than rows, not more rows than columns
False, because a 5x3 matrix can have 3 pivot columns, meaning its 3 columns can be linearly independent
questions.explanation: False. A 5x3 matrix has 3 columns, each in R^5. Those 3 columns can be linearly independent if the matrix has 3 pivot columns. Having more rows than columns does not force dependence.

questions.question: The null space of an m x n matrix A is a subspace of R^m.
options: True, because solutions to Ax=0 are outputs of A, which land in R^m
True, because the null space is defined through the rows of A, each of which has m entries
False, because the null space of A consists of vectors x satisfying Ax=0 where x is in R^n, so Null(A) is a subspace of R^n
False, because the null space is the zero subspace and is therefore not contained in any specific R^m
questions.explanation: False. The null space is Null(A) = {x in R^n : Ax = 0}. The vectors in question are inputs x, which come from R^n, not outputs in R^m. Null(A) is a subspace of R^n.

questions.question: The column space of an m x n matrix A is a subspace of R^n.
options: True, because the n columns of A each span a direction in R^n, placing the column space inside R^n
True, because A maps R^n to itself, so its column space must also be a subset of R^n
False, because the column space is only defined for square matrices where m equals n
False, because each column of A has m entries, so the column space is a subspace of R^m
questions.explanation: False. The columns of an m x n matrix each have m components, so they are vectors in R^m. The column space Col(A) is therefore a subspace of R^m, not R^n.

questions.question: If the columns of a matrix A are linearly independent, then the equation Ax=b has at most one solution for any vector b.
options: True, because linearly independent columns mean Ax=0 has only the trivial solution, which implies Ax=b can have at most one solution for any b
True, because linearly independent columns force A to be a square invertible matrix, guaranteeing a unique solution for every b
False, because linear independence of columns only restricts the homogeneous case and has no effect on nonhomogeneous systems
False, because Ax=b could still have two solutions if b happens to lie exactly on the boundary of the column space
questions.explanation: True. If the columns are linearly independent, Ax=0 has only the trivial solution, meaning there are no free variables. If Ax=b and Ax=c are both solutions then A(b-c)=0, so b=c. Therefore Ax=b has at most one solution.

questions.question: A set of vectors {v1, v2, ..., vk} is linearly independent if and only if none of the vectors is the zero vector.
options: True, because any set containing the zero vector is automatically dependent, and if no vector is zero then independence holds
True, because nonzero vectors by definition cannot satisfy the dependence equation c1v1 + ... + ckvk = 0 with nonzero coefficients
False, because nonzero vectors can still be linearly dependent; for example, (1,0) and (2,0) are both nonzero yet one is a scalar multiple of the other
False, because linear independence requires every pair of vectors to be orthogonal, not merely nonzero
questions.explanation: False. Being nonzero is necessary but not sufficient for linear independence. For example, v1=(1,0) and v2=(2,0) are both nonzero, but v2=2v1, so the set {v1,v2} is linearly dependent.

questions.question: If an n x n matrix has n distinct eigenvalues, then it is diagonalizable.
options: True, because n distinct eigenvalues force the matrix to be symmetric, and all symmetric matrices are diagonalizable
True, because distinct eigenvalues each produce a linearly independent eigenvector, giving the n independent eigenvectors needed to form P in A = PDP^{-1}
False, because diagonalization also requires the eigenvectors to be mutually orthogonal, which distinct eigenvalues do not guarantee
False, because diagonalizability requires each eigenvalue to have algebraic multiplicity greater than 1, which n distinct eigenvalues cannot provide
questions.explanation: True. Eigenvectors from distinct eigenvalues are always linearly independent. With n distinct eigenvalues you get n linearly independent eigenvectors, which is exactly the condition for diagonalizability.

questions.question: If lambda is an eigenvalue of A, then the eigenspace for lambda is equal to the null space of the matrix (A - lambda*I).
options: True, because the eigenspace for lambda consists of all vectors v satisfying Av = lambda*v, equivalently (A - lambda*I)v = 0, which is exactly Null(A - lambda*I)
True, because subtracting lambda from the diagonal of A shifts all eigenvalues to zero, making every eigenvector land in the standard null space
False, because the eigenspace for lambda is the column space of (A - lambda*I), not its null space
False, because eigenspaces are defined through the characteristic polynomial and have no direct connection to null spaces
questions.explanation: True. Av = lambda*v rearranges to (A - lambda*I)v = 0, so the eigenspace is exactly the solution set of this homogeneous system, which is Null(A - lambda*I).

questions.question: A square matrix is diagonalizable if and only if it has n distinct eigenvalues.
options: True, because n distinct eigenvalues are the only configuration that provides the n independent eigenvectors required for diagonalization
True, because the characteristic polynomial of an n x n matrix has at most n roots, and diagonalization requires all of them to be distinct
False, because diagonalizability requires only that the matrix be symmetric, regardless of whether eigenvalues are distinct
False, because a matrix can be diagonalizable even with repeated eigenvalues; the identity matrix has only one eigenvalue but is already diagonal
questions.explanation: False. The correct condition is that for every eigenvalue, the geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic multiplicity. The identity matrix I has only one eigenvalue (lambda=1 with algebraic multiplicity n) yet is perfectly diagonalizable.

questions.question: The rank of a matrix equals the number of nonzero rows in its row echelon form.
options: True, because each nonzero row in REF contains exactly one pivot, so the count of nonzero rows equals the number of pivots, which is the rank
True, because rank is also equal to the number of zero rows in RREF subtracted from the total row count
False, because rank is defined as the number of free variables, not the number of nonzero rows
False, because the number of nonzero rows in REF can vary depending on which row operations are chosen, so it cannot uniquely define rank
questions.explanation: True. Every nonzero row in REF contains a leading entry (pivot), and each pivot is in a different column. The number of pivots is the rank, and pivots and nonzero rows are in one-to-one correspondence.

questions.question: The rank-nullity theorem states that rank(A) + nullity(A) = m, where A is an m x n matrix.
options: True, because the m rows of A each contribute to either the rank or the nullity, so their sum must equal m
True, because rank measures how many rows are nonzero and nullity measures the rest, and together they account for all m rows
False, because the rank-nullity theorem only applies to square matrices where m equals n
False, because the rank-nullity theorem states rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, where n is the number of columns of A
questions.explanation: False. The rank-nullity theorem relates to the number of columns: rank(A) + nullity(A) = n. Rank is the number of pivot columns and nullity is the number of free columns, and every column is one or the other.

questions.question: If A is an invertible n x n matrix, then the null space of A contains only the zero vector.
options: True, because invertible matrices have determinant zero, forcing all solutions to Ax=0 to collapse to the trivial one
True, because A invertible means A has n pivots and no free variables, so the only solution to Ax=0 is x=0
False, because even invertible matrices retain free variables that contribute nonzero vectors to the null space
False, because the null space of any n x n matrix always contains at least one nonzero vector
questions.explanation: True. A is invertible means A has full rank n and no free variables. The only solution to Ax=0 is x = A^{-1}*0 = 0, so Null(A) = {0}.

questions.question: Row operations on a matrix do not change its column space.
options: True, because row operations are reversible and must therefore preserve every subspace associated with the matrix
True, because row operations represent left-multiplication by invertible matrices, which preserves the span of the columns
False, because row operations change the actual entries of each column vector, so the span of the columns can change
False, because column spaces are preserved only by column operations, not row operations, which affect rows only
questions.explanation: False. Row operations change the column vectors themselves. For example, the matrix [[1,2],[2,4]] has column space spanned by (1,2), but after row reducing to [[1,2],[0,0]] the column space is spanned by (1,0) instead. The row space and null space are preserved by row operations, but not the column space.

questions.question: If two matrices have the same RREF, then they have the same null space.
options: True, because the null space is exactly the solution set of Ax=0, row reduction preserves that solution set, so two matrices sharing the same RREF have the same null space
True, because two matrices with the same RREF must be equal to each other, so their null spaces trivially agree
False, because two different matrices can share the same RREF only when they have different null spaces
False, because the null space depends on the original matrix entries, not on the reduced form
questions.explanation: True. Row reduction preserves the solution set of a homogeneous system. Since both matrices row-reduce to the same RREF, they define the same set of solutions to Ax=0 and therefore have identical null spaces.

questions.question: A linear transformation T: R^n -> R^m is one-to-one if and only if T(x) = 0 has only the trivial solution.
options: True, because any function between vector spaces is automatically one-to-one when the codomain R^m is larger than the domain R^n
True, because T is one-to-one exactly when distinct inputs produce distinct outputs, which is equivalent to the kernel of T being {0}, meaning T(x)=0 implies x=0
False, because being one-to-one requires T to be onto as well, and T(x)=0 having only the trivial solution says nothing about surjectivity
False, because T(x)=0 having only the trivial solution means T is the zero map, which is never one-to-one
questions.explanation: True. T is one-to-one iff T(u) = T(v) implies u = v, which is equivalent to T(u - v) = 0 implying u = v, i.e., Ker(T) = {0}. This is exactly the condition that T(x)=0 has only the trivial solution.

questions.question: A linear transformation T: R^n -> R^m represented by matrix A is onto if and only if the columns of A span R^m.
options: True, because T is onto means every vector in R^m is achieved by some input, which is precisely the condition that every b in R^m can be written as Ax, i.e., the columns span R^m
True, because being onto requires n to equal m, and when A is square its columns automatically span R^m
False, because being onto only requires A to have at least m rows; the columns do not need to span R^m specifically
False, because columns spanning R^m only guarantees the system is consistent, not that every output in R^m is reachable
questions.explanation: True. T is onto iff every b in R^m has at least one x with T(x) = Ax = b, which holds precisely when the column space of A equals R^m, i.e., the columns of A span R^m.

questions.question: If A and B are both n x n invertible matrices, then AB is also invertible.
options: True, because (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}, so an explicit inverse of AB can always be constructed when A and B are individually invertible
True, because the product of any two square matrices of the same size is always invertible
False, because the product AB could fail to be square if the sizes change during multiplication
False, because even if A and B are individually invertible, their product may have a zero determinant if their column patterns cancel
questions.explanation: True. When A and B are both invertible, (AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1}) = A(BB^{-1})A^{-1} = AIA^{-1} = I, so B^{-1}A^{-1} is the inverse of AB.

questions.question: A subset W of R^n is a subspace if and only if it contains the zero vector, is closed under vector addition, and is closed under scalar multiplication.
options: True, because any set satisfying all three conditions must span all of R^n, making it a valid subspace
True, because these three conditions are exactly the definition of a subspace: every linear combination of vectors in W must stay in W, and the three conditions capture this precisely
False, because a subspace only needs closure under linear combinations; containing the zero vector is redundant since it follows from scalar multiplication
False, because subspaces require a fourth condition: the set must have finite cardinality to be well-defined
questions.explanation: True. These three conditions are the standard definition of a subspace. A subset W is a subspace iff it contains 0 and is closed under both vector addition and scalar multiplication.

questions.question: If v1 and v2 are orthogonal nonzero vectors, then {v1, v2} is linearly independent.
options: True, because if c1v1 + c2v2 = 0, taking the dot product with v1 gives c1*||v1||^2 = 0, so c1 = 0 since v1 is nonzero, and similarly c2 = 0
True, because orthogonal vectors always lie in perpendicular subspaces, which guarantees they span the full ambient space
False, because orthogonality is a geometric property with no bearing on linear independence
False, because two vectors can be orthogonal while one is a nonzero scalar multiple of the other
questions.explanation: True. Suppose c1v1 + c2v2 = 0. Dot both sides with v1: c1(v1 dot v1) + c2(v1 dot v2) = c1||v1||^2 = 0. Since v1 is nonzero, c1 = 0. The same argument with v2 gives c2 = 0, proving independence.

questions.question: An orthonormal set of vectors is always linearly independent.
options: True, because an orthonormal set is in particular an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors, and any set of nonzero mutually orthogonal vectors is linearly independent
True, because unit-length vectors by definition point in directions that cannot be combined to reach the zero vector
False, because orthonormality only ensures dot products are 0 or 1 and says nothing about whether a nontrivial linear combination can equal zero
False, because an orthonormal set can include opposite-sign unit vectors whose combination is zero, creating dependence
questions.explanation: True. Orthonormal vectors are all nonzero (norm 1) and mutually orthogonal. The same dot-product argument used for orthogonal nonzero vectors shows all coefficients in any dependence relation must be zero.

questions.question: The least squares solution to Ax = b always exists and is always unique.
options: True, because the function ||Ax - b||^2 is strictly convex, so it always has a unique global minimum
True, because the normal equations A^TAx = A^Tb always have exactly one solution for any matrix A and any vector b
False, because while a least squares solution always exists, it is unique only when the columns of A are linearly independent; otherwise there are infinitely many solutions
False, because the least squares solution does not always exist; when b is orthogonal to the column space no minimizing vector can be found
questions.explanation: False. A least squares solution always exists (the normal equations are always consistent), but uniqueness requires the columns of A to be linearly independent so that A^TA is invertible. If columns are dependent, A^TA is singular and there are infinitely many least squares solutions.

questions.question: In the diagonalization A = PDP^{-1}, the diagonal entries of D are the eigenvalues of A.
options: True, because the columns of P are the eigenvectors of A and the diagonal entries of D are the corresponding eigenvalues, by the definition of diagonalization
True, because the diagonal entries of D are always either 0 or 1, representing which standard basis vectors are eigenvectors of A
False, because the diagonal entries of D are the singular values of A, which only equal the eigenvalues when A is symmetric
False, because the diagonal entries of D equal the trace of A divided by n, not the individual eigenvalues
questions.explanation: True. In A = PDP^{-1}, the columns of P are eigenvectors and D is diagonal with the corresponding eigenvalues on the diagonal. This is the definition of diagonalization.

questions.question: If the columns of an n x n matrix A are linearly independent, then A is invertible.
options: True, because independent columns force A to be symmetric, and all symmetric square matrices are invertible
True, because for a square matrix, n linearly independent columns means A has full rank n, which is equivalent to A being invertible
False, because linear independence of columns only ensures Ax=0 has the trivial solution; the matrix could still fail to be invertible for other reasons
False, because an n x n matrix can have independent columns but still be singular if its rows are linearly dependent
questions.explanation: True. For a square n x n matrix, having n linearly independent columns is equivalent to having rank n, which is equivalent to being invertible. All of these conditions are equivalent for square matrices.

questions.question: Row operations on a matrix do not change its null space.
options: True, because row operations preserve the solution set of any linear system Ax=0, so the null space remains identical throughout row reduction
True, because row operations only affect the column space of a matrix, leaving all other associated subspaces unchanged
False, because adding a multiple of one row to another introduces new constraints that can shrink the null space
False, because row operations change the matrix itself, and since the null space is computed from the matrix, it must change as well
questions.explanation: True. Each elementary row operation corresponds to multiplying on the left by an invertible matrix E. Since E is invertible, EAx = 0 iff Ax = 0, so the solution set of the homogeneous system, i.e., the null space, is unchanged.

questions.question: A matrix A is its own inverse if and only if A^2 = I.
options: True, because A being its own inverse means A^{-1} = A, so A*A = A*A^{-1} = I, giving A^2 = I
True, because squaring a matrix always produces the identity matrix whenever the matrix is invertible
False, because A^2 = I is the condition for A to be a projection matrix, not a self-inverse matrix
False, because A^2 = I means A is nilpotent, which is the opposite of being invertible
questions.explanation: True. A is its own inverse iff A^{-1} = A. Substituting into AA^{-1} = I gives A*A = I, i.e., A^2 = I. Conversely, if A^2 = I then A*A = I, so A^{-1} = A.

questions.question: If lambda = 0 is an eigenvalue of A, then A is not invertible.
options: True, because if 0 is an eigenvalue then Av = 0 for some nonzero v, which means Ax=0 has a nontrivial solution, so A cannot be invertible
True, because eigenvalues are the diagonal entries of the matrix, so having 0 as an eigenvalue means A has a zero on the diagonal, making it singular
False, because eigenvalues measure the stretching factor of A, and a zero eigenvalue just collapses one direction without affecting overall invertibility
False, because A can still be invertible with a zero eigenvalue as long as the corresponding eigenvector is not in the column space of A
questions.explanation: True. If 0 is an eigenvalue, there exists a nonzero vector v with Av = 0*v = 0. This means Ax=0 has the nontrivial solution x=v, so A has a zero determinant and is not invertible.

questions.question: In an LU factorization of A (without row swaps), L is a lower triangular matrix with 1s on the diagonal and U is the row echelon form of A.
options: True, because LU factorization always exists for every square matrix and these exact forms of L and U are guaranteed in every case
True, because in the standard LU factorization, L records the row elimination multipliers with 1s on its diagonal, and U is the upper triangular result after forward elimination
False, because L must be upper triangular and U must be lower triangular in the LU factorization
False, because U in the LU factorization is the RREF of A, not just the REF
questions.explanation: True. In the LU factorization (when no row swaps are needed), L is a unit lower triangular matrix whose off-diagonal entries are the multipliers used during elimination, and U is the resulting upper triangular matrix, which is a row echelon form of A.

questions.question: The geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue can exceed its algebraic multiplicity.
options: True, because when an eigenspace is large, its dimension can grow beyond what the characteristic polynomial degree suggests
True, because repeated eigenvalues always force a larger eigenspace than the multiplicity count from the characteristic polynomial
False, because geometric and algebraic multiplicities are always equal by the spectral theorem, so neither can exceed the other
False, because the geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue is always less than or equal to its algebraic multiplicity
questions.explanation: False. The geometric multiplicity is always at most equal to the algebraic multiplicity. It can be strictly less (which is why a matrix with repeated eigenvalues may fail to be diagonalizable), but it can never exceed the algebraic multiplicity.

questions.question: An n x n matrix A is diagonalizable if and only if for every eigenvalue, its geometric multiplicity equals its algebraic multiplicity.
options: True, because this condition ensures each eigenspace contributes exactly enough independent eigenvectors to fill the full set of n independent eigenvectors required to form P in A = PDP^{-1}
True, because equal multiplicities force all eigenvalues to be distinct, and n distinct eigenvalues always guarantee diagonalizability
False, because diagonalizability also requires the matrix to have all real eigenvalues, not just matching multiplicities
False, because geometric and algebraic multiplicities are always equal for every matrix, so this condition is trivially satisfied and cannot determine diagonalizability
questions.explanation: True. A is diagonalizable iff it has n linearly independent eigenvectors. This holds iff each eigenspace (geometric multiplicity) is large enough to match the number of times the eigenvalue appears as a root of the characteristic polynomial (algebraic multiplicity).

questions.question: If A is an invertible matrix, then A^T is also invertible.
options: True, because transposing a matrix preserves its determinant, so the nonzero determinant needed for invertibility is maintained
True, because (A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T, so A^T has an explicit inverse whenever A is invertible
False, because transposing swaps rows and columns, which can destroy the pivot structure needed for invertibility
False, because the inverse of a transpose is only defined when the matrix is symmetric, and invertible matrices are not always symmetric
questions.explanation: True. Since det(A^T) = det(A) is nonzero, A^T is invertible. Explicitly, (A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T, which can be verified: A^T*(A^{-1})^T = (A^{-1}*A)^T = I^T = I.

questions.question: For an m x n matrix A, the column space Col(A) and the null space Null(A) together span all of R^n.
options: True, because the rank-nullity theorem states rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, so Col(A) and Null(A) must together account for all n dimensions of R^n
True, because every vector in R^n can be decomposed into one part lying in Col(A) and one part lying in Null(A)
False, because Col(A) is a subspace of R^m while Null(A) is a subspace of R^n; they live in different spaces and cannot together span R^n
False, because only the null space spans R^n on its own; the column space is orthogonal to it and contributes nothing
questions.explanation: False. Col(A) consists of vectors in R^m (outputs) and Null(A) consists of vectors in R^n (inputs). They cannot be combined to span R^n because they live in different ambient spaces. The correct pairing is: Row(A) and Null(A) are orthogonal complements in R^n.

questions.question: If A is a 4x3 matrix with rank 3, then the equation Ax=b has a solution for every b in R^4.
options: True, because rank 3 means A has 3 linearly independent columns, which is enough to span all of R^4
True, because a matrix with full column rank can always solve Ax=b for any vector b in the target space
False, because A has 4 rows but only 3 pivot columns, so Col(A) is 3-dimensional and does not fill R^4; some vectors b have no solution
False, because Ax=b can only have a solution for every b in R^4 when A is a square 4x4 invertible matrix
questions.explanation: False. For Ax=b to be solvable for every b in R^4, the columns of A must span R^4. But A is 4x3, so Col(A) has dimension at most 3, which is a proper subspace of R^4. There will always be vectors b outside Col(A).

questions.question: All vectors in an orthonormal basis have Euclidean length equal to 1.
options: True, because orthonormality requires each vector to be a unit vector with norm 1 in addition to being mutually orthogonal with every other vector in the set
True, because the Gram-Schmidt process always automatically scales every vector to unit length, so any basis produced by it is orthonormal
False, because orthonormal only means the vectors are mutually orthogonal; having unit length is a separate optional constraint
False, because the lengths of vectors in an orthonormal basis must sum to 1, but individually they can be any positive value
questions.explanation: True. An orthonormal set satisfies two conditions: (1) all vectors have norm 1, and (2) any two distinct vectors are orthogonal. Both conditions together define orthonormality.

questions.question: For matrices A and B where the product AB is defined, (AB)^T = A^T * B^T.
options: True, because the transpose distributes over matrix multiplication the same way it distributes over addition
True, because transposing each factor individually always preserves the product structure of the original multiplication
False, because the transpose of a product is only defined when both A and B are square matrices
False, because the correct identity is (AB)^T = B^T * A^T; the order of the factors must be reversed when transposing a product
questions.explanation: False. The correct rule is (AB)^T = B^T * A^T. The factors are reversed, just as with inverses: (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}. Forgetting to reverse the order is a common mistake.

questions.question: A homogeneous system of linear equations always has at least one solution.
options: True, because homogeneous systems are always consistent since every row of A has at least one nonzero entry
True, because x = 0 always satisfies Ax = 0, so the trivial solution is always available regardless of the matrix A
False, because a homogeneous system with more equations than unknowns is overdetermined and may have no solution
False, because a homogeneous system only has solutions when A has fewer rows than columns
questions.explanation: True. For any matrix A, substituting x=0 gives A*0 = 0, so the zero vector is always a solution. This is called the trivial solution, and it guarantees that every homogeneous system is consistent.
